extraction.name: CADS: A Comprehensive Anatomical Dataset and Segmentation for Whole-Body Anatomy in Computed Tomography
extraction.description: CADS is an open-source framework for whole-body CT segmentation comprising a large-scale dataset of 22,022 CT volumes with complete annotations for 167 anatomical structures, aggregated from over 40 diverse sources across 16 countries. It includes a segmentation model suite (CADS-model) trained on this dataset and a 3D Slicer plugin for clinical use.
extraction.license: Multiple licenses (varies by source dataset; see dataset documentation)

extraction.rai:dataCollection: CT volumes were aggregated from three main sources: (1) large-scale public archives including TotalSegmentator, NLST, CT-RATE, and AbdomenCT-1K; (2) specialized annotation collections from medical imaging challenges (Grand Challenge, MICCAI) and focused research studies; and (3) newly contributed images including 484 anonymized head CTs from Istanbul Medipol University and 586 triphasic contrast-enhanced abdominal CT scans from TUM Klinikum Rechts der Isar. The collection spans more than 100 imaging facilities across 16 countries, collected between 2007 and 2024.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionType: Secondary Data analysis, Manual Human Curator, Web Scraping, Physical data collection
extraction.rai:dataCollectionMissingData: Only 21% of the 22,022 CT volumes contain any annotations; approximately 79% of the initial collection does not include any manual annotations.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionRawData: CT volumes from public archives (TCIA, Grand Challenge, MICCAI challenges), including TotalSegmentator (1,203 volumes), NLST (7,172 scans), CT-RATE (3,134 scans), AbdomenCT-1K (1,062 scans), HaN-Seg, SAROS, VISCERAL, and various TCIA oncology studies; plus 484 newly acquired head CTs from Istanbul Medipol University and 586 triphasic contrast-enhanced abdominal CTs from TUM Klinikum Rechts der Isar.
extraction.rai:dataManipulationProtocol: For patient privacy in newly acquired hospital head CT scans, a Gaussian filter (σ=5 voxels at 1.5 mm spacing) was applied to facial regions to obscure identity while preserving structural integrity.
extraction.rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: A three-step pipeline was applied: (1) reorientation of all images to standard RAS (Right-Anterior-Superior) convention; (2) resampling to uniform 1.5 mm isotropic resolution; (3) simplification of affine transformation matrices by removing rotation and translation components, preserving only scaling and shear.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Annotations were generated through a multi-stage pipeline: (1) pseudo-labeling using specialized models trained on high-quality annotations from established datasets for nine anatomical groups; (2) shape-based quality control using neural implicit functions to detect and exclude outlier pseudo-labels; (3) multi-strategy label generation using three model 'flavors' (GT-flavor, Pseudo-flavor, Shape-flavor) with statistical ranking to select the best annotation per structure; (4) assembly of final labels prioritizing original GT annotations over pseudo-labels. Additional manual annotations were contributed by three in-house medical research assistants and a radiation oncologist for the VISCERAL Gold Corpus dataset.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationPlatform: MIM software (for University Hospital Zurich evaluation cohort reference annotations)
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: For each anatomical structure, the best-performing model flavor (GT, Pseudo, or Shape) was selected via statistical ranking using Dice Similarity Coefficient as primary metric and HD95 as secondary metric, with Shapiro-Wilk normality tests, Levene's variance equality tests, and ANOVA/Welch's ANOVA/Kruskal-Wallis tests with post-hoc comparisons (Tukey's HSD or Dunn's test). Original GT annotations took highest priority and replaced pseudo-labels when available.
extraction.rai:machineAnnotationTools: nnU-Net framework (for specialized segmentation models and pseudo-labeling); neural implicit functions / auto-decoder (for shape-based quality control); vesselFM (foundation model for tubular structure detection used in rib segmentation refinement); SimNIBS MRI atlas with ANTs non-rigid transformation (for brain structure annotation via registration)
extraction.rai:personalSensitiveInformation: All newly acquired head and abdominal CT scans are anonymized. Facial features in head CTs are intentionally blurred using a Gaussian filter for privacy. The dataset includes patient data from clinical settings (oncology patients, patients with various pathological conditions).
extraction.rai:dataSocialImpact: CADS aims to advance robust AI solutions in radiology and make comprehensive anatomical analysis accessible to clinicians and researchers. Clinical applications include radiation oncology treatment planning, diagnostic radiology for organ volume quantification, and large-scale population studies. The framework bridges technical capabilities and clinical applications, contributing to AI-integrated healthcare workflows.
extraction.rai:dataBiases: The dataset may have limited representation of pathological conditions with atypical anatomical variations, as the shape-based quality control excludes such cases from training. Class imbalance exists, with some structures (e.g., upper cervical vertebrae C1-C5) appearing less frequently across the 22,022 volumes. Existing public datasets used as sources contain known annotation errors, particularly in ribs and vertebrae.
extraction.rai:dataLimitations: Known limitations include: (1) exclusion of pathological cases with atypical anatomical variations due to shape-based quality control; (2) coverage limited to head to knees, excluding hands and feet; (3) limited training data for certain structures (e.g., buccal mucosa in fewer than 1,000 scans); (4) small organs below 0.5 mL affected by CT resolution limits; (5) facial features are anonymized, limiting facial analysis applications; (6) specific segmentation issues: brain mask too inclusive, optic chiasm under-segmented, heart omits superior portions, rectum appears shorter than anatomical extent, trachea limited to air content, vena cava imprecise.
extraction.rai:dataUseCases: Primary use cases: training and validation of whole-body CT segmentation models; radiation therapy planning; diagnostic radiology; anatomical landmark detection; cross-modality registration; anatomy-guided image synthesis; longitudinal organ tracking; personalized anatomical modeling; large-scale population studies. The dataset is split into non-overlapping training and test sets for model development and evaluation.

name.evidence: CADS : A Comprehensive Anatomical Dataset and Segmentation for Whole-Body Anatomy in Computed Tomography

description.evidence: At its core is a large-scale dataset of 22,022 CT volumes with complete annotations for 167 anatomical structures, representing a significant advancement in both scale and coverage, with 18 times more scans than existing collections and 60% more distinct anatomical targets.

url.evidence: Our CADS-dataset, comprising paired CT volumes and curated whole-body annotations, is publicly accessible via https://huggingface.co/datasets/mrmrx/CADS-dataset

license.evidence: Users of the CADS-dataset must comply with the individual licenses and terms of use for each source dataset, and properly cite the original works. For detailed information about individual dataset licenses, please refer to our dataset documentation and the original publications cited within this paper.

rai:dataCollection.evidence: Our data collection strategy systematically consolidates CT scans and annotations from three main sources: (1) large-scale public archives including TotalSegmentator [27] (1,203 annotated volumes with comprehensive coverage of 104 anatomical structures)... (2) specialized annotation collections from medical imaging challenges... and (3) newly contributed images and annotations, comprising manual annotations of critical OARs on the VISCERAL dataset, 484 newly acquired anonymized head CTs, and 586 triphasic contrast-enhanced abdominal CT scans.

rai:dataCollectionType.evidence: We aggregate our dataset from diverse sources, including medical imaging challenges (e.g., Grand Challenge, MICCAI challenges) and public repositories such as The Cancer Imaging Archive (TCIA). We further enhance the dataset with two new CT collections. First, we include 484 anonymized head CT scans from patients aged ≥18 years from Istanbul Medipol University... Second, we incorporate 586 triphasic contrast-enhanced abdominal CT scans from TUM Klinikum Rechts der Isar.

rai:dataCollectionMissingData.evidence: Starting with a diverse collection of 22,022 CT volumes, where only 4,695 (21%) contain partial annotations from public sources... Consequently, approximately 79% of our initial collection does not include any manual annotations.

rai:dataCollectionRawData.evidence: The CADS-dataset aggregates 22,022 CT volumes from 40 diverse sources... large-scale public archives including TotalSegmentator [27] (1,203 annotated volumes), the National Lung Screening Trial (NLST [40], 7,172 scans), CT-RATE [41] (3,134 scans), and AbdomenCT-1K [42] (1,062 scans)... 484 newly acquired anonymized head CTs... 586 triphasic contrast-enhanced abdominal CT scans.

rai:dataCollectionTimeframe.evidence: The geographic diversity of the dataset spans 16 countries across multiple continents, integrating data from over 100 medical centers collected between 2007 and 2024.

rai:dataManipulationProtocol.evidence: For patient privacy in newly acquired hospital head CT scans, we apply a Gaussian filter (σ= 5 voxels at 1.5 mm spacing) to facial regions. This relatively strong blurring effectively obscures identity while preserving the overall structural integrity required for anatomical analysis near the face area.

rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol.evidence: We implement a three-step pipeline: First, we reorient all images to the standard RAS (Right-Anterior-Superior) convention. Second, we resample to a uniform 1.5 mm isotropic resolution... Third, we simplify the original affine transformation matrices by removing rotation and translation components, preserving only scaling and shear.

rai:dataAnnotationProtocol.evidence: Our annotation methodology (Figure 2) first standardizes the data by aligning all images to consistent orientation and 1.5 mm isotropic resolution. We then implement a multi-stage annotation process. First, we organize the 167 target structures into nine anatomical groups and develop specialized models for each group... These specialized models then perform whole-body pseudo-labeling... To ensure annotation quality, we implement two key safeguards: automated outlier detection of pseudo-labels in shape space using neural implicit functions... and multi-strategy label generation through an ensemble selection mechanism.

rai:dataAnnotationPlatform.evidence: For this cohort, reference annotation masks were either generated using MIM software and validated by medical doctors, or directly contoured by radiation oncologists following standard clinical protocols.

rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis.evidence: For each anatomical structure, we implement a performance-driven process (Algorithm 1) to identify the most reliable model flavor. We evaluate segmentation quality using Dice Similarity Coefficient (Dice) as the primary metric and 95-percentile Hausdorff distance (HD95) as a secondary metric... We perform statistical tests (significance threshold p<0.05) to assess if the observed Dice score differences between three flavors are statistically significant.

rai:machineAnnotationTools.evidence: We employ the nnU-Net framework [22] to train specialized models for each body group. These models then generate pseudo-labels for all 167 structures... We train an auto-decoder on ground-truth multi-class segmentation labels... The auto-decoder is based on implicit neural representations... We begin by leveraging vesselFM [107], a foundation model initially developed from 3D blood vessel segmentation... We generate annotations by registering Han-Seg CT scans with the SimNIBS MRI atlas [97] using ANTS non-rigid transformation.

rai:personalSensitiveInformation.evidence: For patient privacy in newly acquired hospital head CT scans, we apply a Gaussian filter (σ= 5 voxels at 1.5 mm spacing) to facial regions... Due to privacy considerations, facial features are intentionally anonymized, limiting applications requiring detailed facial analysis... we include 484 anonymized head CT scans from patients aged ≥18 years from Istanbul Medipol University.

rai:dataSocialImpact.evidence: By making our large-scale dataset, our segmentation models, and our clinical software tool publicly available, we aim to advance robust AI solutions in radiology and make comprehensive anatomical analysis accessible to clinicians and researchers alike... in radiation oncology, it can streamline treatment planning through rapid organ delineation; in diagnostic radiology, it can enable automated organ volume quantification and detection of subtle anatomical changes; and for research applications, it can facilitate large-scale studies across diverse populations and conditions.

rai:dataBiases.evidence: A primary limitation of our approach concerns the exclusion strategy in our shape-based quality assessment. By directly excluding segmentations identified as low-quality from the training process, we potentially eliminate cases involving pathological conditions that present atypical anatomical variations... In the CADS-dataset, this class imbalance can be observed in structures like the uppermost cervical vertebrae (C1-C5) that appear less frequently across the 22,022 volumes... Our evaluation on the TotalSegmentator dataset... reveals inaccuracies in these ground-truth labels across many structures, particularly evident in ribs and vertebrae segmentations.

rai:dataLimitations.evidence: A primary limitation of our approach concerns the exclusion strategy in our shape-based quality assessment... While CADS spans from head to knees, future work can extend to additional regions (e.g., hands, feet)... limited training data for certain structures (e.g., buccal mucosa appears in less than 1,000 scans with only 30 ground-truth annotations)... very small organs (volumes below 0.5 mL) where standard CT resolution limits and partial volume effects impact accuracy... Due to privacy considerations, facial features are intentionally anonymized, limiting applications requiring detailed facial analysis.

rai:dataUseCases.evidence: serving dual purposes: enabling the development of the whole-body segmentation CADS-model and supporting further research in medical imaging... On the technical side, it can support anatomical landmark detection, cross-modality registration, and anatomy-guided synthesis. For clinical applications, it enables a wide range of uses including longitudinal organ tracking, personalized anatomical modeling, radiation treatment planning, and large-scale population studies.
